kicker: A Second Examination of the Grand Schemes of our Governing Gentlemen
headline: ALTO: OR, THE NINETY-BILLION DOLLAR IRON DREAM OF A GOVERNMENT THAT CANNOT MANAGE AN APP
deck: In which the Printer considers the Liberal Ministry's magnificent High-Speed Railway — announced without Parliament's consent, planned without a cost-benefit analysis, and projected to ruin the public finances of every Province save the two that shall chiefly benefit from it.
source_topic: The Liberal Ministry's announcement of Alto, the Crown corporation tasked with constructing a high-speed railway from Quebec City to Toronto at a cost of $60–90 billion.
body:
## The Ledger of Broken Promises

California's high-speed rail, approved at $46 billion in 2008, has ballooned past $174 billion after nearly two decades — and not one mile of track has been laid.

Britain's HS2, budgeted at £37 billion in 2015, has surpassed £100 billion in estimated costs. Its northern legs have been cancelled outright.

Canada's own Trans Mountain Pipeline expansion was estimated at $7.4 billion. Final cost: over $34 billion — a four-fold overrun.

ArriveCan, a simple telephone application, was commissioned for $80,000 and delivered at a cost of $60,000,000.

These are the hands into which the Ministry proposes to entrust ninety billions of the people's money.

---

There is a particular variety of political vanity which this Printer has observed across a long life spent in the press-room and in the public arena: the vanity of the Grand Project. It is the vanity of the man who, unable to mend the leaking roof of his house, proposes instead to demolish it and construct in its place a palace — financed, naturally, upon credit, and to be completed by the time his grandchildren come of age. The present Ministry has contracted this vanity in its most acute form, and the instrument of their delusion goes by the name of Alto.

Alto — such is the name bestowed upon the Crown corporation charged with constructing a high-speed railway from Quebec City to Toronto, with trains to travel at three hundred and twenty kilometres per hour, and the whole magnificent enterprise to be accomplished at a cost somewhere between sixty and ninety billion dollars. That the lower figure already represents the most optimistic estimate, and that every comparable project in the civilized world has exceeded its initial budget by a factor of two or three, ought to give the most enthusiastic friend of rapid transit some cause for sobriety. But sobriety is not the present fashion in Ottawa.

The project was announced — not debated in Parliament, not subjected to the scrutiny of elected representatives, not put to the people in any form — but announced, by the outgoing Prime Minister Trudeau in the February of last year, a few weeks before he vacated the office he had already been compelled to relinquish. A man leaving a burning house does not typically pause to commission expensive renovations; yet this departing minister saw fit to bind the public treasury to a scheme of ninety billions before handing the keys to his successor. It was, one must concede, a gesture of considerable audacity.

> "A Government that spent $60,000,000 on a telephone application budgeted at $80,000 now asks the public to trust it with a railway costing ninety billions. Reader, at that rate of overrun, the true cost of Alto would equal the gross domestic product of the entire Dominion."

Let us now examine what, precisely, is being offered for this sum. Alto, its promoters assure us, will carry twenty-five million passengers annually. It will reduce travel time between Toronto and Montreal to three hours and seven minutes. It will boost Canada's gross domestic product by thirty-five billions per year. These are handsome promises. But when the careful men of McGill University examined the underlying arithmetic, they found that the project will only achieve profitability — if that word may be stretched to cover the circumstance — after fifty-three billion dollars in public subsidy and forty-four years of operation. Let that figure rest in the mind of the reader for a moment: fifty-three billions in subsidy. That is roughly equivalent to the entire annual revenue this government collects through the Goods and Services Tax. And the thirty-five billion dollars of annual GDP growth promised by Alto's own boosters? It amounts, upon examination, to approximately two per cent of the combined gross product of Ontario and Quebec — that is to say, roughly what those provinces are already projected to grow this year, without a dollar of rail investment whatsoever.

The Globe and Mail's editorial board, not generally noted for Revolutionary sympathies, has observed that Alto's projected benefits to travellers over sixty years of operation are pegged by the project's own administrators at approximately forty-nine billion dollars — a sum which is, in the unsparing language of arithmetic, less than the cost of building the thing. A railway that costs more than the total value it will ever deliver is not, by the usual standards of political economy, an investment. It is a monument. And monuments, however noble their intent, are traditionally financed by those who commission them — not by the unborn children of provinces that shall never see a single station.

---

This brings us to the most grievous injustice embedded in this project, and one which this Printer wishes to place before the people of the western provinces, of the Atlantic shore, and of every region of this Dominion that lies beyond the charmed corridor between Quebec City and Toronto. Alto's benefits — whatever they may prove to be — will accrue overwhelmingly to Ontario and Quebec, those two provinces which between them hold the balance of seats in Parliament and the ear of every government that has sat at Ottawa within living memory. Its costs — that is to say, the debt service on ninety billions borrowed in the name of all Canadians — will be distributed with fine democratic impartiality across every household in the land. The farmer of Saskatchewan, who shall never ride this train, shall pay for it. The fisherman of Newfoundland, a thousand miles from the nearest proposed station, shall pay for it. The working family of British Columbia, who might prefer that their federal government invest in something of relevance to their own lives, shall pay for it.

There is a name for this arrangement in the honest language of political economy. It is called the taxation of the many for the benefit of the few, administered by a government which has never submitted this particular expenditure to Parliamentary debate, which announced it without consulting the great pension funds that might actually finance it, which has yet to release a detailed cost-benefit analysis to the public, and which is — even at this late hour — unable to say with any precision where the ninety billions will come from, beyond the general and inexhaustible source that governments have always preferred: the national credit, to be repaid by posterity.

> "The benefits of Alto fall upon two provinces. Its debts fall upon thirty-eight million Canadians. This Printer calls that by its plain name: tribute."

The Ministry's defenders will protest that this country requires bold infrastructure investment, and that the timid counsel of accountants must not be permitted to strangle the aspirations of a nation. This Printer does not dispute the first proposition. Canada's passenger rail service is, as any traveller will readily confirm, an embarrassment to a wealthy country. Via Rail's trains crawl at speeds that the railways of France, Japan, and Spain surpassed forty years ago. The case for investment in rail — real investment, prudent and proportionate — is not a controversial one. But there is a profound difference between mending the leaking roof and building a palace. The government had been studying a sensible alternative for nearly a decade: High-Frequency Rail, a more modest proposal that would have placed more trains on improved existing track and served more Canadians at a fraction of the cost. It was practical, deliverable, and bore the cardinal merit of being achievable within a human lifetime. The outgoing Prime Minister set it aside in favour of Alto's gleaming vision, as a man exchanges a reliable horse for a thoroughbred he has no stable to house and no jockey to ride.

Nor is this Printer reassured by the international comparisons with which Alto's advocates seek to dazzle the public. Japan's Shinkansen — that marvel of engineering and national will — connects a corridor of sixty million people across five hundred and fifteen kilometres. Alto's core route links metropolitan populations of approximately ten millions across a comparable distance. The ridership base is, in the brute language of mathematics, one-sixth the size. California attempted its high-speed railway; after eighteen years and costs tripled from forty-six billions to over one hundred and seventy-four, no track has been laid. Britain's HS2 has consumed over a hundred billions and been partially cancelled. Canada's own Trans Mountain Pipeline — a far simpler undertaking than a thousand kilometres of electrified railway through the varied and litigious geography of two provinces — exceeded its original budget by four hundred per cent. The government that oversaw that overrun is the government now proposing to manage Alto.

---

And then there is the matter of the land. Alto requires new, dedicated, and supremely straight track — for a train travelling at three hundred and twenty kilometres per hour cannot, as the Crown corporation's own Chief Executive has candidly explained, tolerate curves. It must therefore pass in a nearly undeviating line through the farms, woodlots, villages, and properties of the Quebec-Windsor corridor, acquiring whatever it needs by the ancient and sovereign power of expropriation. "If people are reluctant," said Mr. Martin Imbleau, the Chief Executive of Alto, with a frankness this Printer cannot but respect for its honesty if not its charity, "there is of course some recourse with the expropriation process." A hundred and fifty years ago, it was the Family Compact that felt entitled to dispose of the people's land without their full and free consent. Today it wears a different coat and carries a different title, but the disposition is the same: the great project shall go forward, and those in its path may apply for compensation.

The people of the corridor communities — those citizens whose farms, properties, and livelihoods lie in Alto's projected path — organized themselves into an association and commissioned a national survey. They found that only one Canadian in four strongly supports this project, that one in five remains entirely undecided, and that the project's enthusiasts are concentrated, almost entirely, in Ontario and Quebec. They found, further, that the project was announced without consulting Parliament and without public debate. They have asked, as free citizens of a democratic country have every right to ask, for genuine consultation before expropriations proceed. Whether they shall receive it remains, at this writing, an open question.

This Printer has one final observation, and it concerns the nature of the thing itself. High-speed rail is not, in principle, an unworthy ambition. But a worthy ambition improperly executed, inadequately costed, inequitably distributed, imposed without Parliamentary mandate, and assigned to a government whose record of managing large public undertakings gives every rational person cause for alarm, is not a worthy ambition in practice. It is an act of hubris dressed in the language of national pride. The Ministry has spent three billion nine hundred million dollars on the planning phase alone — money already committed to a design process expected to last four to five more years, before a single spike is driven or a single passenger carried. The full construction will not be complete, on the project's own timeline, until some time between 2041 and 2044. That is, Reader, nearly two decades from today — if all goes to plan, which it will not.

The people of this country deserve a railway. They deserve one that serves them honestly, that is proportionate to the revenues available to pay for it, that does not conscript the unborn into debt for the gratification of the present Ministry's desire to be remembered as builders. They deserve one that was debated in their Parliament, costed with their scrutiny, and approved by their representatives. What they have been given, instead, is Alto: a sovereign name for a borrowed dream, a monument to the ambition of men who will be long retired — or long departed — before the first train runs, and who shall bear none of the consequences if it does not.

This Press demands what it has always demanded: the truth, the full accounts, and the consent of the governed. Nothing more, and nothing less.
issue_date: York, Upper Canada — The Seventh of May, in the Year 2026

kicker: On the Great & Gilded Fraud now Perpetrated upon the People
headline: THE CANADA STRONG FUND: A SOVEREIGN NAME FOR A BORROWED SWINDLE
deck: Wherein the Printer examines Mr. Carney's vaunted Wealth Fund, and finds therein no Wealth, no Fund, and very little that may rightly be called Canadian at all — save the Bill which the People must pay.
source_topic: Prime Minister Mark Carney's announcement of the Canada Strong Fund, a proposed sovereign-wealth-style vehicle to be capitalised through borrowing.
body:
Reader, you have been presented with a marvel. In these days of economic uncertainty and national anxiety, our Minister-President — that erstwhile Governor of the Bank of England, that darling of Davos, that polished instrument of international Finance — has announced that Canada shall at last have what Norway has: a Sovereign Wealth Fund. He stood before a gleaming locomotive at the Museum of Science and Technology in Ottawa — very apt, for he, too, is a machine built to impress — and declared that this new Fund would be the people's own. "It will be your Fund," said he. Reader, when a man of great means tells a man of modest ones that a thing is his, take care to count your fingers after the handshake.

Let us examine this prodigy with the same plain candour that this Press has always employed. Norway's great Fund — held up by Mr. Carney as his model and his inspiration — was built upon something that all honest men will recognize as the necessary precondition of a Wealth Fund, to wit: wealth. The Norwegians, blessed with offshore oil, did not spend those revenues upon the appetite of the present moment. They stored them. They invested them abroad — deliberately abroad, lest the very weight of so much capital overheat their own economy. Their Fund forbids domestic investment by solemn rule. Today that Fund commands some three trillion dollars and covers nearly a quarter of Norway's annual expenditures from its returns alone. It is a monument to the virtues of prudence, patience, and public ownership wisely exercised.

> "A Sovereign Wealth Fund requires, as its very foundation, Sovereignty and Wealth. Mr. Carney's Canada Strong Fund possesses neither, and borrows freely in the hope that no one shall notice the absence of both."

Mr. Carney's Fund is something altogether different — though the name is the same, as a counterfeiter's shilling bears the same face as a true one. The Government of Canada does not possess surplus revenues. It has not possessed them for the better part of two decades. Its net worth, if so flattering a term may be applied to so dismal a ledger, stands in the negative to the tune of one trillion and four hundred billion dollars. A negative net worth! And yet from this abyss of obligation, Mr. Carney proposes to conjure twenty-five billion dollars — not from oil revenues salted away, not from surpluses accumulated in years of prudent governance — but from borrowing. He would place the debt upon the backs of the very people he addresses as the Fund's beneficiaries and owners. He would write their names upon a credit instrument and call it a gift.

This is not a Sovereign Wealth Fund. It is, as the sharp-tongued men of the press and the counting-house have already observed, a leveraged investment vehicle staffed by bureaucrats — a kind of private equity fund, minus the private capital and minus the equity, financed instead by the public treasury and the goodwill of future generations yet unborn, who have not been consulted and cannot vote. It invests not abroad, where risk is hedged and returns are diversified, but exclusively in Canadian projects — meaning that when our domestic economy contracts, as it has done and shall do again, the losses shall compound themselves with savage efficiency upon both the Fund and the nation at once.

---

Now, there are those who shall accuse this Printer of mere factional carping, of opposing Mr. Carney because opposition is our trade. Let them examine the critics more carefully. It is not the Reformers alone who raise these objections. Economists of the first rank, financial commentators of no particular political complexion, and even the great pension funds of this country — who were not, we note with some astonishment, so much as consulted before the announcement — have each in their own manner expressed bewilderment. What is this Fund for, precisely? If the projects it shall finance are commercially viable, why cannot private capital — which Mr. Carney assures us will invest alongside the Fund — finance them without the public guarantee? And if the projects are not commercially viable, then what we have is not an investment vehicle but a subsidy engine dressed in the respectable clothes of finance.

The people of this country deserve an honest answer to that question. They will not easily obtain one, for the details of this Fund were withheld at the time of its grand announcement, as they have so often been withheld when grand announcements prove, upon scrutiny, to be grand theatre. The Fund's purposes shift with the questions put to it. One day it is nation-building infrastructure; the next, clean energy; the next, advanced manufacturing; the next, a retail investment vehicle into which ordinary Canadians may pour their modest savings — their children's educations, their retirements, their small accumulated hopes — into projects that the private sector has already deemed unworthy of its attention. Is this the inheritance Mr. Carney has prepared for them?

> "When a Minister announces a Fund built on Debt and calls it Wealth, when he offers the People a stake in projects that no private man will touch, and names this generosity — then has the language of public finance been debased as surely as any clipped coin."

There is, moreover, a darker concern which this Printer would place before the public, and which the polished language of financial prospectuses will not easily address. Every student of political economy knows the great peril of a government fund that selects among projects, for it must necessarily reward some men and neglect others. The selection of projects is the selection of favourites. The governance of such a fund — however independent its board, however commercial its stated mandate — will be tempted by political necessity at every turn. A mine in a marginal constituency, a pipeline that serves a particular interest, a hydrogen facility that happens to employ the workers of a province about to vote — these are the pressures against which no fund charter has yet proven entirely proof. The best-constructed sovereignty in the world cannot fully insulate public money from political desire. And Mr. Carney's Fund, we are told, will be explicitly connected to nation-building priorities chosen by the Cabinet itself. This is independence in name only.

We have been here before. Not in these precise circumstances, perhaps — for each generation invents its own peculiar forms of the same ancient corruptions — but in spirit and in kind. This Printer has, across many years of publishing, observed how power clothes itself in the rhetoric of the public good. The Family Compact of an earlier age did not announce its intentions as the oppression of the common man; it announced them as good order, prosperity, and loyal progress. Today the language is different — it speaks of sovereignty, of nation-building, of competing with America — but the mechanism is the same: the concentration in few hands of decisions that touch the pockets and prospects of all.

Canada is a wealthy country. Abundantly, embarrassingly wealthy in land, in water, in mineral, in forest, in the ingenuity of its people. But that wealth has never translated cleanly into the hands of those who produced it, and it will not do so now through the invention of a Fund that borrows money to invest it in projects selected by the same political class that has presided over decades of deficits and the gradual hollowing-out of the public household. The workers of this country do not need their government to gamble on their behalf with borrowed capital while offering them a retail instrument by which they may, if they wish, gamble too. They need the conditions — sound regulation, honest taxation equitably applied, the rule of law uncaptured by private interest — within which their own industry may flourish.

---

Mr. Carney is a man of formidable intelligence and international stature. This Printer will grant him that without reservation, for it would be as dishonest to deny his abilities as to pretend that abilities alone constitute wisdom in governance. But there is a particular danger in the very clever man who, having mastered the mechanisms of global finance, mistakes those mechanisms for the foundations of national life. A sovereign wealth fund is a tool. Like all tools, its virtue lies entirely in the use to which it is put, the conditions under which it operates, and the honesty with which its custodians account for it to those in whose name it acts. On each of these counts, the Canada Strong Fund — as presently described, or rather, as presently undescribed, for the details remain yet to be furnished — raises more questions than it answers.

The people of this dominion are not children, to be dazzled by a locomotive and a noble name. They understand debt. They feel it in their mortgages and their grocery bills and the interest charges on the credit extended to them by the very financial institutions that Mr. Carney once regulated. To tell them that borrowing twenty-five billion dollars is equivalent to saving it — that a Fund built on debt is a Fund built on wealth — is to treat them as something less than the free, rational, and morally serious citizens that this Press has always believed them to be.

We close with a simple demand, which this Printer makes not in the name of faction or party, but in the name of that plain accountability without which no free government may long endure: Show us the details. Open the books. Name the projects, name the governance, name the costs, name the risks, and let the people judge. If this Fund is what Mr. Carney says it is — a genuine instrument of public wealth, transparently managed, free from political interference, prudently structured — then let that case be made in the clear light of full disclosure, and this Printer will say so. But if, as so many careful observers already suspect, it is a borrowed speculation dressed in patriotic clothes, then the people of Canada deserve to know that too — before they are asked to pay for it.

They are, after all, the ones who shall.

headline: RUSSIAN GHOSTS SUMMONED TO SMOTHER WESTERN GRIEVANCE
deck: The Liberal Compact and its CTV scribes brand Alberta discontent foreign disinformation rather than confront the equalisation robbery and Ottawa's energy noose
body:
Once more the Family Compact dons new red livery and cries foreign agent; this time the charge is levelled by a study whose authors scraped social-media posts for the words Wexit and Alberta independence, then declared a Russian hand behind every prairie murmur. The same scribes who cheered when the Emergencies Act crushed lawful truckers now warn that discussion of resource theft and carbon levies must be Moscow mischief. Ye toadies of the PMO, your panic betrays the truth: the West has cause enough without any foreign whisper.

The report, issued under the banner of an Ottawa-linked institute and reliant upon keyword trawls rather than proof of rouble transfers, follows the ancient tactic. In 1826 the Compact called reformers Yankee tools; today the same bloodline calls them Russian amplifiers. Grievances over equalization payments that drain Alberta's treasury to feed Laurentian sinecures, over federal land grabs dressed as climate policy, and over vaccine mandates enforced by decree are thereby transformed from legitimate complaints into tainted treason. No mention is made of the far larger sums flowing from Beijing-linked entities into favoured academic and media channels.

The methodology is as thin as the old Compact's loyalty oaths. Algorithms flag repetition; repetition is labelled amplification; amplification is labelled Russian. Thus the farmer watching his propane costs rise under the carbon levy, the rig worker whose job vanishes to satisfy central edicts, and the mother unable to heat her home become unwitting dupes. The press, fattened on federal bailout cheques, prints the smear and calls it scholarship.

Western Canadians ask only the plain rights long denied them: control over their own resources, an end to fiscal transfers that punish productivity, and a Parliament that does not rule the provinces by Order-in-Council. These demands predate any alleged Kremlin tweet. They were born in the wheat fields and the oil patch, not in some St. Petersburg troll farm.

Yet the Compact cannot answer them. To do so would require loosening its grip on the nation's purse and its grip on the nation's story. So it reaches for the familiar tar-brush. Foreign disinformation, it cries, while ignoring the domestic kind it manufactures daily through subsidised outlets and compliant regulators. The yeomanry of Alberta grow weary of the libel; they will read their own accounts in their own papers, and they will remember who sought to brand honest dissent as enemy work.
source_topic: CTV News article citing a study on alleged Russian amplification of Alberta separatism

headline: THE JUDGES OF THE COMPACT — CARNEY’S PARTISAN BENCH
deck: Ottawa’s latest judicial appointments continue the ancient racket of Liberal loyalists donning the ermine while the people’s courts are packed with placemen
body:
O ye toadies of the PMO and the velvet chair of the Justice Minister, how long shall the people of these Provinces endure a bench chosen not by merit but by the secret ledgers of Liberalist? The latest announcements from Sean Fraser’s department, proclaimed in the first days of May, name yet another clutch of donors and party familiars to the Federal Court and the superior benches of the Provinces; and the Macdonald-Laurier Institute has but now torn away the veil, showing that seventy-two parts in every hundred of these appointments since the pretended reform still bear the mark of the red ledger.

The Compact of old chose its judges from the sons of the rectory and the counting-house; the new Compact chooses them from the same sons now dressed in the livery of the Laurentian banks and the Ottawa law firms that feast upon the public purse. When the premiers of Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan and Alberta demanded some share in the naming of those who shall judge their people, the Minister answered with the old cant of “independence” and “Judicial Advisory Committees” whose very names are kept from the light of day. What independence is that which hides its members and its minutes behind the curtain of the Privy Council Office?

The yeoman who tills the soil of Saskatchewan, the fisherman who risks the Banks, the trucker who hauls the grain, all stand before these judges; yet the judges themselves stand before no man save the Prime Minister who raised them. The secret ballot is mocked when the very men who interpret the laws that guard that ballot are first required to prove their fealty by cheque and contribution. The press that once thundered against such things now draws its subsidy from the same hand that signs the commissions; thus the outrage is muffled and the people are told that all is well.

I say it is not well. While the Compact packs the courts, the plain laws of the land are bent to serve the interests of the chartered banks, the carbon-tax collectors, and the land speculators who bid up every acre around the cities. The Constitution itself is become a plaything for men who have never faced an open poll. Let the farmers and the tradesmen of the West remember how their forefathers broke the old Family Compact; let them now demand that the new one be broken likewise, and that judges be named only by open process, by provincial legislatures, and by the free voice of the people whose liberty they are sworn to protect.

For every fresh appointment that smells of the party bag, another link is forged in the chain that binds the Provinces to the central tyranny. The ink is scarcely dry upon the commission before the new judge is called upon to decide some matter touching the very ministers who placed him there. Such a system cannot stand; and if the men of Parliament will not end it, the men of the ridings must.
source_topic: the ongoing partisan judicial appointments under the Carney Liberals and the opacity of the federal selection process as exposed in April 2026 reports
issue_date: York, Upper Canada — The Second of May, in the Year 2026

headline: THE BOUGHT VOTE AND THE NEW FAMILY COMPACT
deck: Mark Carney’s Liberal machine gobbles up Opposition defectors while the people’s franchise lies in rags
body:
O ye electors of Canada! The same ring that once fattened upon the King’s lands and the people’s taxes has changed its livery from blue to red and calls itself the Liberal Party. In the month just past, three more members who stood against the Compact at the last election have crossed the floor to sit at the table of the Prime Minister. Marilyn Gladu, Michael Ma, and Chris d’Entremont have sold their votes for the promise of sinecures and the favour of the court. By these treacheries Mark Carney now stands one seat from a majority that the ballot box denied him.

The Compact of 1826 held its power by appointment and marriage. The Compact of 2026 holds it by defection and cheque-book. The yeoman of the West, the fisherman of the Maritimes, the small manufacturer who cannot meet the carbon levy nor the interest on his mortgage—these are told their voices count for less than the whispered bargain struck in the corridors of the House. The secret ballot is become a jest when the man elected to oppose the government can be bought for a committee chair or a judgeship in waiting.

We remember the broken press of 1826. The types were scattered and the editor jailed because he printed the truth about the ring that ruled Upper Canada. Today the same ring rules through the CRTC, through the media bailout that keeps the metropolitan press in thrall, and through the judicial appointments handed out by the Minister of Justice to men and women whose loyalty has already been tested in the caucus room. The names change; the method remains the same.

The trucker who hauls grain across the Prairies, the parent who cannot find a house at any price, the Indigenous nation still waiting for treaty lands—these pay the price while the defectors feast. Provincial sovereignty is mocked by decrees from Ottawa that arrive faster than the mail. Free speech is regulated by tribunal. Property is taxed to subsidise the very banks whose chairs lunch weekly with the Finance Minister.

Let the people mark the date. April 8, 2026, when the fourth defection secured the Liberal grip. Let them remember that no man who crosses the floor for place or pension ever returns to the side of the plain folk. The ink is not yet dry on the writs that sent these men to Parliament. Already the type is being reset to proclaim the new majority.

O Canada, thou hast been sold again by thy own representatives. The press that should thunder against it draws its subsidy and holds its tongue. The compact grows fat. The people grow poor. But the types still stand in the cases, and the old fire is not quenched.
source_topic: the April 2026 defections of Conservative MPs to the Liberal caucus under Prime Minister Mark Carney, securing a near-majority
issue_date: York, Upper Canada — The Twenty-Eighth of April, in the Year 2026
